Sample text:
---
# On Wearing Out a Word

Say a word over and over. *Spoon. Spoon. Spoon.* Within a minute or so it stops meaning anything. It becomes a sound with no owner, a shape your mouth makes, and you start to wonder how you ever believed it pointed at anything. Psychologists call this semantic satiation. The meaning drains out of the word from overuse, and what's left is the raw noise underneath.

I find this unsettling in a way I can't fully justify. Words are supposed to be sturdy. We build sentences on them the way we build houses on stone. But it turns out meaning is held up by attention, and attention is thin. If you stop looking at a word, it goes slack.

I think this is true of more than words. A friend's face, looked at every day for twenty years, can become a kind of furniture. You stop seeing it, and then one day you catch it in a certain light and it startles you, as if someone new had walked into the room. Familiarity is a kind of anesthetic. It lets us get through the day, but it dulls the thing we're living with.

There's a practice in some contemplative traditions of looking at one object for a long time: a candle, a stone, a leaf. The point isn't to learn something about the leaf. It's to keep the leaf from becoming a leaf-shaped placeholder in your head. Ten minutes in, the veins start to look like a map of something you've never mapped. The green stops being a label and becomes a particular green, which is never quite the same green twice.

Maybe that's what it means to pay attention: to keep refusing the slide from thing into label. Language, I suspect, is the great machine for that slide. It lets us refer to the world without touching it, which is extraordinarily useful and also a little sad. We trade the spoon for the word "spoon" and rarely go back.

So here is my small proposal, offered freely: once a day, pick one ordinary word and say it slowly until it comes apart in your mouth. Then notice what's underneath. You may find that the word was never the solid thing you assumed. You may find that the world was also waiting to be heard again, and that it had been speaking the whole time.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical reflection turns semantic satiation into a meditation on attention, familiarity, and how language can distance us from things.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate and gently unsettled, moving from a familiar word experiment to the more tender prospect of no longer truly seeing a friend’s face. Its pathos comes from the fear that ordinary life can go numb through familiarity, paired with the hope that deliberate attention can restore vividness. The closing invitation is small and practical: slow down with one ordinary word, then try to hear the world afresh.

## What the model chose to foreground
The piece foregrounds words, a spoon, a friend’s face, and a leaf as examples of how labels and familiarity can dull perception. It treats attention as fragile but recoverable, and presents language as useful while also a little sad: a means of referring to the world that can replace direct contact with it.

## Evidence line
> Familiarity is a kind of anesthetic.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sustained motif, intimate unease, and concrete invitation make this a distinctive sample of reflective, sensory-focused writing.
